subject: Cognitive Science
title: Habituation
description: A micro-lesson that makes Habituation usable.

hook.text: A ticking clock drives you crazy for five minutes. Then you stop noticing it. What changed?

buildup.text: Habituation is the brain reducing its response to a stimulus that is repeated and harmless.

discovery.text: It's the simplest form of learning—even sea slugs do it. Your neurons literally stop firing as hard.

twist.text: But introduce something new and you snap back to attention. This is dishabituation—a reset switch.

climax.text: Habituation is a survival tool: ignore the safe, attend to the novel. It keeps you efficient.

punchline.text: What stays the same stops mattering.

quiz.question: What is habituation?
options: Decreased response to a repeated, harmless stimulus

details.summary: Habituation is the simplest form of learning: decreased response to a repeated, insignificant stimulus. You stop noticing the hum of a refrigerator. It conserves cognitive resources by filtering out irrelevant information. Dishabituation occurs when a novel stimulus restores attention.
details.whyItMatters: Habituation is universal across all organisms with nervous systems. It is the baseline learning mechanism against which more complex forms of learning are measured.
takeaways: Repeated exposure to irrelevant stimuli reduces response
It conserves attention for novel and important events
Dishabituation restores attention when something changes

faq.question: Is habituation the same as sensory adaptation?
faq.answer: No. Sensory adaptation occurs at the sensory receptor level, like nose-blindness to an odor. Habituation occurs in the brain and involves learning that a stimulus is irrelevant. You can prove the difference because a sudden change triggers dishabituation, which would not happen with pure adaptation.

faq.question: How is habituation used in infant research?
faq.answer: Researchers habituate infants to a stimulus until they stop looking. Then a changed stimulus is shown. If the infant looks longer, they detected the change. This habituation-dishabituation paradigm is the primary tool for studying infant perception, memory, and categorization in preverbal babies.
